newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile scorns Argentine suggestion on weapons sales.
newsitem.headline: Chile scorns Argentine suggestion on weapons sales.

text.p: Chile on Wednesday ridiculed an Argentine suggestion that rich countries should voluntarily freeze their sales of sophisticated military weapons to South America to prevent a regional arms race.

Chilean Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza, whose country is busily replacing its vintage war materiel with newer European weapons, said asking others to stop selling weapons to South America was like asking them to stop selling wine as a way to curb alcoholism.

"It's like saying 'Please help us to stop drinking by banning the sale of wine.' No, no, this is strictly our problem. If the countries of South America want disarmament, then don't buy arms," he told reporters.

Argentine Vice President Carlos Ruckauf was quoted as saying recently that countries that deal in sophisticated weapons should voluntarily stop selling them to South America to prevent an arms race from developing in the region.

Asked specifically about Ruckauf's comments, Insulza said "they have no business going around asking others to please put an embargo on weapons sales to Latin America. That strikes us as the sort of procedure from the past that should not be repeated."
Nonetheless he said he "appreciated the spirit of the proposal which, without a doubt, is aimed at disarmament."

Ruckauf made the suggestion as Chile moved closer to a deal for purchase of two Scorpene-type submarines from a French-Spanish consortium. Chile has also been shopping for F-16-style fighter jets, looking at various U.S. and European models, and has bought 67 German-built tanks from Belgium.

Chile expects to close the $500 submarine deal with French-Spanish group DCNI-Bazan by the middle of June but has still not ruled out a competing German model, Defence Minister Edmundo Perez Yoma said last week.

Insulza denied the submarine purchase meant Chile was seeking to take a military advantage over its neighbours, and said he had received no official word of concern from Argentina or Brazil about the purchase.

"There are always certain quarters or the news media that say such things, but I haven't heard any official opinion from those governments on those issues," he said. "Besides, I don't see how swapping two submarines for two submarines can be an arms race, unless they want us to continue going around in 40-year-old submarines."
"I don't think you can turn over the responsibility for disarmament and arms-limitation agreements (in Latin America) to third countries in the developed world," he said.

Argentina, which has cut its defence spending to the bone while Chile maintains one of the region's highest rates, has been particularly rankled by Chile's plans to replace older aircraft with advanced jets like the F-16, news reports in Santiago have said.

A U.S. official said last month said the Clinton administration had given U.S. manufacturers permission to bid for the Chilean jet purchase, in which U.S. maker Lockheed will be in competition with French and Swedish makers, the Santiago paper El Mercurio reported.
